correctness.rationale: The canonical free-space operator has norm equal to the Lipschitz constant: the universal property gives the upper bound and normalized molecules attain the pairwise ratios. On unordered pairs, distinct-cycle return times are lcm(a,b), and same-cycle return times divide a cycle length. All periods 3 through n are realized by neighboring vertices of a cycle, 2 by a transposition plus a fixed point, and 1 by the identity. On an orbit of length ell, the complementary forward path of length (-k) mod ell bounds the distance gain by that length times epsilon, independently of the defect of f^k. The capped descending ramp after the tested jump attains the bound with denominator 1 and satisfies all one-step inequalities; every symmetric off-diagonal assignment in [1,2] is a metric. The only pair for n=2 is fixed. For epsilon>0, the times with norm envelope 1 are exactly multiples of lcm(1,...,n), proving minimal period even after saturation. Epsilon=0 instead gives the constant profile. The initial linear range follows by separating orbit lengths above k from those at most k, whose residues are at most k-1. POWER_CHECK.py was inspected, not executed; the recorded finite diagnostic is supplementary, and the proof does not depend on it.

value.rationale: Sharp finite-space plasticity gives a natural reason to ask how norm gains accumulate when only the original map's defect is controlled. The result quantifies when all admissible powers are isometric, when saturation is possible, and how gains recur instead of growing with an iterated Lipschitz bound. The exact least period can be much larger than any individual pair period; this is useful information not supplied by the one-step constant.
